source: Hollingworth & Beck (2016) Memory-based attention capture when multiple items are maintained in visual working memory
finding: Two held colours can both capture attention. Capture was larger when two distractors matched two held colours than when one matched one held colour (gap-location task). This argues against a one-item-only template.
numbers: Two experiments, N=24 each. Gap task: Mem-1/Match-1 68 ms (t=4.27); Mem-2/Match-1 44 ms (t=2.30, p=.03); Mem-2/Match-2 124 ms (t=5.90); 124 vs 68 ms t=2.36, p=.034. Singleton task: Mem-1/Match-1 58 ms; Mem-2/Match-1 6 ms (p=.72); Mem-2/Match-2 51 ms (t=3.14). Memory accuracy 84.6% (1 item) vs 68.4% (2 items) in gap task.
quote: Instead, multiple VWM representations can interact simultaneously with perceptual selection.
limits: The two tasks disagree: the singleton task showed no two-colour advantage (authors: reason not clear). Only set sizes 1 and 2. Capture measures guidance against the observer's wishes, so it may not mirror ordinary use.
agent_relevance: More held lessons can bias what is noticed at once, though each adds less. A scaffold that carries several lessons should expect combined pull on attention.

source: Hollingworth & Beck (2016), boundary data: presence versus match
finding: Mere presence of a memory-coloured item is not what drives the effect in the gap task: a non-matching coloured distractor did not slow search there, but it did in the singleton task.
numbers: Match-0 vs No-Color: p=.20 and p=.29 (gap task) but reliable in the singleton task. Search accuracy 98.3% and 96.1%. Outliers beyond 2.5 SD removed: 2.3% and 2.9%. Gap task search slope above 35 ms/item.
limits: Paradigm choice changes what counts as capture. Design differences shift results by tens of ms.
agent_relevance: When we test fixation in an agent, a control for plain presence of a distractor is needed, not only match versus no match.

source: Large-scale replications of Van Moorselaar, Theeuwes & Olivers (2014) and Hollingworth & Beck (2016): Can you have multiple attentional templates?
finding: Exp 1 replicated capture with one held colour but found no capture with two held colours (Bayes factors favour no effect). Exp 2 replicated the Hollingworth-Beck pattern: capture at load 2, stronger with two matches.
numbers: Exp 1: 56 analysed of 66; 26,180 of 32,670 trials kept. Load 1: location-match BF10=36.5, mismatch BF10=1.19e5. Load 2: BF10=0.163 and 0.117 (substantial evidence for no difference). Capture at load 1 in 43/56 people; load 2 in 28/56 (about chance). Memory accuracy 76% vs 67%. Exp 2: 56 analysed of 81; Match-2 vs Match-1 BF10=158.5; Match-1 vs unrelated BF10=3.86; 42/56 stronger on Match-2.
quote: A single demonstration of at least one attentional template being active with a memory load of two
limits: The two experiments differ in number of distractors (1 vs 2), memory display time (1000 vs 250 ms) and target definition. Online data, heavy exclusions in Exp 2. Exp 2 had no load-1 baseline. Authors say neither template account is clearly supported.
agent_relevance: Held-item guidance at higher load is fragile and design-dependent. Do not assume more held lessons means more reliable bias.

source: Hollingworth (2022) The architecture of interaction between visual working memory and visual attention (chapter in Visual Memory)
finding: Review of the capture literature. Holding an item in memory is not enough for guidance: often only a subset is in an active template state. The active state can span more than one item. Early null results (Downing & Dodds 2004; Olivers 2009; Houtkamp & Roelfsema 2006) were likely underpowered and never tested for evidence in favour of the null.
numbers: Conclusions: (1) maintenance not sufficient for guidance; (2) active items can be set by task demands; (3) active state can span multiple items. Two-item capture replicated several times (Chen & Du 2017; Fan 2019, 2021; King & Macnamara 2020; Zhang 2018; Zhou 2020).
limits: Review by a lab that also produced much of the evidence. Open questions: upper limit on active items, and what separates active from passive items.
agent_relevance: Held content biases noticing mainly when it is in an active state, and that state can be set by task demands. For an agent, whether a lesson is flagged active in the working prompt may matter more than whether it is stored.

source: Bahle, Beck & Hollingworth (2018) The architecture of interaction between visual working memory and visual attention
finding: Five experiments with larger samples and more sensitive measures found consistent capture by a secondary held item even while another item served as the search template. Supports the multiple-item view over the single-item view.
numbers: Exp 3 (natural scenes): colour-matching distractors fixated on 23.6% of trials vs 11.0% when mismatching (about double); effect strongest on the first saccade. Capture on manual RT and fixation probability, for colour and shape memory, abstract arrays and photographs. Control (N=40) with no memory demand tested low-level priming.
limits: Capture effects were small relative to guidance by the target template. Two partial experiments with N=17 and 18 showed no reliable capture (footnote).
agent_relevance: Held items bias early looking (first saccade) more than final outcome. In an agent, fixation may show in the first moves of a plan even if the final answer is unchanged.

source: Bahle, Thayer, Mordkoff & Hollingworth (2020) The architecture of working memory: parallel, coactive guidance from multiple remembered objects
finding: Race-model-inequality tests showed redundant-target responses too fast for any one-at-a-time or independent-parallel account. Two held features guided attention together and their effects summed.
numbers: 3 experiments; violations of the race-model inequality in all cases predicted by the multiple-item hypothesis.
limits: Applies to cued search targets, not unwanted capture. Exact RT numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Two held cues add up rather than compete one at a time. A prompt with two matching lessons may bias more strongly than one.

source: Niu & Hollingworth (2026) Testing a sensory preactivation account of attention guidance from visual working memory
finding: Guidance needs a memory demand. A colour merely flashed (no need to remember) gave no or weak guidance, while a colour that had to be remembered gave robust guidance. Rules out simple sensory afterglow as the main cause.
numbers: Exp 1 (must remember): match effect about 150 ms at 0 ms ISI rising to about 250 ms at 500 ms ISI. N=24 per experiment. Power based on earlier eta-p2=0.643. Small but reliable guidance from sensory persistence alone in Exps 3 and 4.
limits: Effect had not levelled off by 500 ms. Some no-memory guidance may come from occasional encoding lapses.
agent_relevance: Fixation needs a held representation, not just recent exposure. Text flagged as something to keep (a lesson) may bias more than text only passed through.

source: Sawaki & Luck (2011) Active suppression of distractors that match the contents of visual working memory
finding: EEG found that a task-irrelevant probe matching the held colour produced a Pd (suppression marker), not an N2pc (attention marker). Matching items were detected but actively suppressed.
numbers: N=12. Pd at 250-300 ms: P7/P8 t(11)=3.4, p<.01; PO7/PO8 t(11)=4.0, p<.005. Pd onset about 220 ms vs about 120 ms for salient singletons. 320 matching-probe trials per field. Memory accuracy 78.3%.
quote: the memory-matching probe elicited a Pd component, indicating that it was being actively suppressed
limits: Small sample. Averaged ERPs may hide a trial mix of capture and suppression. Probes were irrelevant so no behavioural cost was measured. One feature (colour).
agent_relevance: Counter to automatic capture: control can veto the pull when matches are known to be useless. An explicit 'this will not help' signal may reduce fixation, but only after the pull is registered.

source: Woodman & Luck (2007) Do the contents of visual working memory automatically influence attentional selection during visual search? (second-hand: Hollingworth 2022 and a student thesis review)
finding: Found no slowing when a distractor matched the held item. In some conditions search was faster with a memory-matching distractor, and the gain scaled with the number of matching items. Interpreted as strategic avoidance.
numbers: Numbers not checked. Hollingworth 2022: advantage scaled with the number of matching items.
limits: Original not opened. Later work (Han & Kim 2009; Olivers 2009) could not reverse the effect except in special cases (see b10).
agent_relevance: Capture is not mandatory: when matches are always distractors, people can learn to use them for rejection.

source: Han & Kim (2009) and Olivers (2009), as summarised in Hollingworth (2022): attempts to reconcile capture with Woodman & Luck
finding: Both teams varied task difficulty, set size and instructions. Capture could be reduced or largely removed, but neither got the reversed (avoidance) direction, except in Han & Kim Exp 4 when search items were previewed 750 ms before the target feature appeared.
numbers: Han & Kim Exp 4 reversal only with a 750 ms preview.
limits: Second-hand summary; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Avoidance of held-content matches seems reactive (needs to see the display first), not pre-set. A scaffold should not count on a stored lesson being filtered out before the problem is seen.

source: Negative-template literature, as summarised in Hollingworth (2022): Arita 2012; Becker 2015; Beck & Hollingworth 2015; Moher & Egeth 2012; Berggren & Eimer 2021
finding: Telling people which colour the target will NOT be sometimes speeds search (Arita 2012) but this failed to replicate in several labs. Eye data show people look at the cued-against items first and avoid them later.
numbers: Becker et al. 2015: no negative-cue advantage in three experiments. Berggren & Eimer 2021, Williams 2020, Cunningham & Egeth 2016 also failed. Hollingworth lab: four unpublished null experiments. Chapter's own quick experiment (N=16, 100 letters): neutral 17.3 s, positive cue 10.2 s, negative cue 11.7 s (about 33% faster than neutral).
limits: Negative advantage appears only when search is hard, many items match, and the cue is useful. Chapter experiment was an online test with N=16. Originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Warning about 'do not do X' lessons: naming a thing to avoid first draws attention to it. Phrase lessons as what to do, and check that negative lessons do not raise use of the named item.

source: Houtkamp & Roelfsema (2006), Downing & Dodds (2004), Olivers (2009): early dual-task nulls, as summarised in Bahle et al. 2018 and Hollingworth 2022
finding: Early tests of whether a second held item captures attention when another item is the search template gave null or ambiguous results.
numbers: No effect sizes in the summaries. Hollingworth: some experiments substantially underpowered; relative evidence for the null never assessed.
limits: Not opened. Bahle 2018 footnote: its own two partial experiments with N=17 and 18 also showed no reliable capture.
agent_relevance: Small agent tests can look like null results. Use many items per condition.

source: Soto, Heinke, Humphreys & Blanco (2005) Early, involuntary top-down guidance of attention from working memory
finding: Founding result: an item held for a later test captured attention in search even though it was never the target and participants knew this.
numbers: Numbers not checked this session.
limits: Original not opened. Hollingworth 2022 groups it with Olivers et al. 2006 as the automatic-capture pair that people could not avoid despite incentive and instruction.
agent_relevance: Core of the fixation concern: held content pulls attention even when it hurts.

source: Dowd, Pearson & Egner (2017); Zhou, Lorist & Mathot (2020), as summarised in a student thesis review
finding: Zhou et al. (two held colours; target or distractor could match) found faster search when the target matched and slower when a distractor matched. Dowd et al. decoded what a person held from their search RTs, even across different people.
numbers: No numbers in the summary.
limits: Secondary source (a student report), low reliability. Its own experiment found the reverse (matching distractors did not slow search; a distractor match occurred on 2/3 of trials, so learned regularity may explain it).
agent_relevance: Cross-person decoding means the bias is regular enough to read out. The reversal at a 2/3 distractor-match rate shows statistical regularity can override capture.

source: Hollingworth & Hwang (2013), as described in Bahle et al. 2018: deprioritised held colours produce no capture
finding: When a postcue marked which of two held colours was likely to be tested, the deprioritised colour produced no observable capture, even when a continuous report showed it was still remembered.
numbers: No numbers extracted.
limits: Described in a paper I opened; the original was not opened.
agent_relevance: A held item can be kept yet inert. Priority marking could be the lever for controlling which lessons bias attention.

source: de Fockert, Rees, Frith & Lavie (2001) The role of working memory in visual selective attention; Lavie load theory
finding: Load theory claim: higher working-memory load reduces control over distractors, so interference rises. Biased competition and the capture work say a held item that matches the distractor adds interference by content. The two views differ in the matching case.
numbers: Numbers not checked this session.
limits: Not opened. Listed to mark the rival prediction named in the subfield row.
agent_relevance: If load alone hurts filtering, long prompts crowd out control. If match drives it, the content of the lessons matters, not their count. A test can vary count and match independently.

source: Shi, Chen, Misra, Scales, Dohan, Chi, Scharli & Zhou (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to a grade-school maths problem sharply cut accuracy for code-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003 under chain-of-thought, least-to-most and program prompting.
numbers: GSM-IC-4K covers all 100 base problems. code-davinci-002 COT overall micro accuracy 72.4%; macro accuracy (right on every variant of a base problem) 6.0%; fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently. Self-consistency over 20 samples: +11 points micro; 0-COT +35.5 points; best macro only 45%. Correct answer in the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems.
limits: 2023 GPT-3-family models only. Single-sentence additions. In-topic, role-name overlap and in-range numbers hurt most.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analog of a distractor that matches held content: distractors sharing topic, names and number ranges hurt most. A scaffold should strip or mark context that overlaps the task but is not needed.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC: mitigation results
finding: Mitigations helped but did not fix it: an instruction to ignore irrelevant information, and exemplars that contain distractors, both raised robustness. A 4-exemplar prompt was better on clean problems but more distractible than a 1-exemplar prompt on problems over 2 steps.
numbers: COT code-davinci-002 micro 72.4% -> 77.8% with instruction; LTM + instruction micro 82.8%, macro 28.0%; PROGRAM 62.2 -> 63.2. Complicated prompts were worse on multi-step problems.
limits: Gains varied by method and model; macro accuracy stays low.
agent_relevance: An explicit 'ignore what is not needed' line and distractor-bearing examples are cheap and tested. Richer lesson prompts can raise distractibility.

source: Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni & Liang (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Models use information best at the start or end of context and worst in the middle (U-shaped curve), even for explicit long-context models.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA drops by more than 20% in the worst position; with 20 and 30 documents worst-case accuracy is below the 56.1% closed-book result. Oracle accuracy 88.3%.
limits: 2023 models. Position effect, not match effect.
agent_relevance: Where a lesson sits changes how much it is noticed. Put active lessons at the edges of the prompt, not the middle.

source: Niu, Yuan, Wang, Saghir & Abdi (2025) Llama see, llama do: a mechanistic perspective on contextual entrainment and distraction in LLMs (ACL 2025)
finding: Closest direct LLM analog of memory capture. Any token seen in the prompt gets a higher logit, even random ones. A small set of attention heads (entrainment heads) drives it. Ablating them reduces the effect.
numbers: Logit shift of the distracting token, Llama-3.1-8B: related +4.08, irrelevant +4.92, random +4.01. Correct-token shift +0.75 with related context, -1.23 irrelevant, -1.17 random. Entrainment heads 2.9% to 10.7% of 1,024 heads (country-capital: 36 heads, 3.5%). Ablation: counterfactual logit gap 7.69 -> 13.20. Factual recall near baseline; in-context-learning tasks drop about 0.2% to 3%. Counterfactual context stronger than factual.
quote: Simply put: llama see, llama do.
limits: Small open models only (GPT-2 XL, Llama-2-7B/13B, Llama-3.1-8B/-Instruct); one dataset (LRE relations); no mitigation; head discovery not fully reproducible (Jaccard 0.317 to 0.548).
agent_relevance: Content in context pulls output toward matching tokens even when irrelevant or random. Fixation by held lessons has a mechanical floor that wording alone may not remove.

source: Kukreja et al. (2026) Better and worse with scale: how contextual entrainment diverges with model size
finding: First scaling laws for entrainment. Meaningful-context entrainment falls with model size; non-meaningful (random, irrelevant) token entrainment rises with size.
numbers: Cerebras-GPT 111M to 13B: distractor-entrainment exponents counterfactual b=-0.330 (R2 0.926), related -0.135, irrelevant +0.091, random +0.217. Pythia 410M to 12B replicates the signs. Largest models about 4x more resistant to counterfactual misinformation but about 2x more likely to copy arbitrary tokens.
limits: Two model families, up to 13B, base models. Not frontier instruction-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Bigger models do not remove the surface-copy pull. Hoping scale fixes fixation is not supported; the scaffold has to.

source: Huang et al. (2025, v2 2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLMs with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring (first-seen number or item pulling later judgement) is common in LLMs. It acts in shallow, early layers. Usual fixes did not remove it. Reasoning models showed the least.
numbers: 22% to 61% of questions anchored depending on model. Anchored-question ratio: Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Phi-3.5-mini 46.3%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%. Llama-3.1-8B baseline 34.7%; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse); self-improving 38.4%; adversarial finetuning 33.3%.
limits: Authors' own metrics and dataset; workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning helps dilute the first-seen item. Fits a rule: reason about the task before held lessons are applied, and check that lessons are not acting as anchors.

source: Adaptive distraction: probing LLM contextual robustness with automated tree search (2025)
finding: Static distractors barely hurt modern models, but adaptively searched distractors (coherent, task-related text) cut accuracy a lot. Prompt fixes gave little; preference training (DPO) helped most.
numbers: Averaged over seven models: accuracy 0.843 original -> 0.323 under attack (52.0% drop; abstract says over 45%). Claude-3.5-Sonnet 0.879 -> 0.495 (38.4% drop). GPT-4o 0.940 -> 0.390. GPT-4o-mini CommonsenseQA 0.857 -> 0.220. GSM-IC static distractors: only 1.8% average drop. Prompt mitigations mostly within +/-0.03. DPO: Phi-3.5-mini 0.195 -> 0.680. Humans judged 87 to 94% of perturbations meaning-preserving.
limits: Attacker-chosen distractors, not natural held content. 6 to 13% of perturbations may shift meaning. Datasets MMLU, CommonsenseQA, OpenbookQA, TruthfulQA.
agent_relevance: Plausible, task-related distractors are the danger. Held lessons are exactly that kind of text. Prompt-only defences were weak, so code-side checks matter.

source: Racing thoughts: explaining contextualization errors in large language models (2024)
finding: Injecting distractor text into the prompt drops accuracy on context-dependent questions toward 50%. A race-condition hypothesis (late tokens read from early tokens before those are contextualised) is supported by patching later-layer states back to earlier layers.
numbers: Accuracy driven to about 50% by distractors in tested sets (Gemma, Llama-2). Backpatching gave 30+ percentage point improvement in some settings (appendix text). Per-model table not extracted.
limits: Small open models; read from PDF text only. Numbers are rough.
agent_relevance: Cue position among distractors changes outcomes. Supports placing key lessons close to the question and keeping noise away from them.

source: Competing explanations across the human literature (synthesis of b01 to b15)
finding: Four rival accounts: (1) single-item template, others inert; (2) multiple-item template; (3) capture then rapid suppression (Sawaki & Luck); (4) learned task statistics decide use or avoidance. Recent large-sample tests favour (2) for capture, with (3) and (4) as moderators.
numbers: Discriminating tests: load-2 capture with two matches vs one (b01, b03); race-model inequality (b06); first-saccade fixation 23.6% vs 11.0% (b05); Pd marker (b08).
limits: b03 shows load-2 capture can fail to replicate in one paradigm, so no account is settled.
agent_relevance: Test fixation in the scaffold with per-lesson on/off conditions rather than assume it.

source: Moderators of memory-based capture (synthesis from opened sources)
finding: Capture is larger with more consolidation time (b07), with more matching items (b01), with eye-tracking measures (b05), and when the held item is task-active. It is smaller or absent when the item is deprioritised (b15), when matches are always distractors (b14), and when search is easy or has a preview stage (b10).
numbers: ISI effect 150 to 250 ms (b07). Fixation 23.6% vs 11.0% (b05). Deprioritised item: no capture (b15).
limits: Instruction, time pressure, training, expertise and culture moderators were not found in sources I could open. Individual-difference results (VWM capacity vs attention scores by paradigm, Dowd et al. 2015) come only from a search-result snippet.
agent_relevance: Levers to test in the scaffold: time before use, count of matches, priority marking, and whether the lesson is useful or always a distractor.
